questions.stem: How is oxidation defined in terms of electron transfer?
options: The sharing of electrons between two atoms
The loss of protons by a chemical species
The loss of electrons by a chemical species
The gain of electrons by a chemical species
questions.explanation: Oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain ('OIL RIG'). Losing protons describes a Brønsted-Lowry acid, not oxidation.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is −2, so four oxygens contribute −8. The ion's charge is −2, so sulfur must be +6. Ignoring the ion's charge gives +8.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of chromium in the dichromate ion, Cr₂O₇²⁻?
questions.explanation: Seven oxygens give −14 and the ion's charge is −2, so the two chromium atoms total +12, which is +6 each. The value +12 forgets to share the total between two atoms.

questions.stem: In the reaction 2Fe²⁺(aq) + Cl₂(aq) → 2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq), which species is the oxidising agent?
options: Fe³⁺
Cl⁻
Cl₂
Fe²⁺
questions.explanation: Chlorine gains electrons, falling in oxidation number from 0 to −1, so it is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent. Fe²⁺ loses an electron, so it is the reducing agent.

questions.stem: Which of these reactions involves no transfer of electrons?
options: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq)
Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq)
questions.explanation: In the precipitation of silver chloride, every element keeps its oxidation number, so no electrons are transferred. The other three each involve one species being oxidised and another reduced.

questions.stem: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺. Which half-equation is balanced?
options: MnO₄⁻ + 4H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 2H₂O
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5e⁻
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 3e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O
questions.explanation: Balance O with 4H₂O, then H with 8H⁺, then charge: the left is +7 before electrons and the right is +2, so 5e⁻ are added to the left. Electrons on the right would make it an oxidation.

questions.stem: Hydrogen peroxide is oxidised to oxygen gas in acidic solution. Which is the correct half-equation?
options: H₂O₂ + 2e⁻ → O₂ + 2H⁺
H₂O₂ → O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻
H₂O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O
H₂O₂ → O₂ + H₂ + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Oxygen goes from −1 in H₂O₂ to 0 in O₂, so two electrons are lost and appear on the right. The second equation is the reduction of H₂O₂ to water, and the last puts electrons on the wrong side.

questions.stem: Acidified permanganate oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, and MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺. Which is the balanced overall equation?
options: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + Fe³⁺
MnO₄⁻ + 4H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 2H₂O + 5Fe³⁺
MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺
questions.explanation: Each MnO₄⁻ gains 5 electrons and each Fe²⁺ loses 1, so 5Fe²⁺ are needed per MnO₄⁻ for the electrons to cancel. The charge then balances at +17 on each side.

questions.stem: Sulfur dioxide is oxidised to sulfate ions in acidic solution. Which is the correct half-equation?
options: SO₂ + 2H₂O → SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
SO₂ + 2H₂O → SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ + 2e⁻
SO₂ + 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → SO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺
SO₂ + O₂ → SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Sulfur rises from +4 to +6, losing 2 electrons. Water supplies the extra oxygen, H⁺ balances hydrogen, and the charge balances: 0 on the left, −2 + 4 − 2 = 0 on the right. Four electrons would leave the right side with charge −2.

questions.stem: A strip of zinc is placed in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. What is observed over time?
options: No change, because zinc is less reactive than copper
A brown coating forms on the zinc and the blue colour fades
A silver coating forms on the zinc and the solution turns blue
Bubbles of hydrogen form and the blue colour becomes darker
questions.explanation: Zinc is the stronger reducing agent, so it is oxidised to colourless Zn²⁺ while Cu²⁺ is reduced to brown copper metal. As Cu²⁺ is used up, the blue colour fades.

questions.stem: Chlorine water is added to colourless potassium bromide solution. What is observed?
options: The solution turns orange-brown as bromine forms
The solution stays colourless as bromide is unreactive
A white precipitate of potassium chloride forms
The solution turns violet as chlorine is reduced
questions.explanation: Chlorine (E° = +1.36 V) is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine (+1.08 V), so it oxidises bromide ions: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. Bromine colours the solution orange-brown; potassium chloride is soluble.

questions.stem: Use E°: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V, Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V. Which mixture reacts spontaneously?
options: Copper wire in silver nitrate solution
Copper wire in zinc sulfate solution
Iodine solution in potassium chloride solution
Silver wire in copper(II) nitrate solution
questions.explanation: A reaction is spontaneous when the oxidising agent is higher in the table than the reducing agent. Ag⁺ (+0.80 V) can oxidise Cu (+0.34 V). Zn²⁺ cannot oxidise copper, iodine cannot oxidise chloride, and Cu²⁺ cannot oxidise silver.

questions.stem: In the incomplete combustion of methane, 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O, how does the oxidation number of carbon change?
options: From 0 to +2
From −4 to +2
From −4 to +4
From +4 to +2
questions.explanation: In CH₄, hydrogen is +1, so carbon is −4. In CO, oxygen is −2, so carbon is +2. Complete combustion in excess oxygen takes carbon further, to +4 in CO₂.

questions.stem: Using E°: F₂/F⁻ +2.87 V, Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, which species is the strongest oxidising agent?
options: Cl⁻
Cu²⁺
F₂
Zn
questions.explanation: The strongest oxidising agent is the species on the left of the half-equation with the most positive E°, which is fluorine. Zinc metal, with the most negative E° couple, is the strongest reducing agent.

questions.stem: Using E°: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V, Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V, Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V, which metal is the strongest reducing agent?
options: Copper
Iron
Zinc
Silver
questions.explanation: The strongest reducing agent is the species on the right of the half-equation with the most negative E°. Zinc gives up electrons most readily, and silver least.

questions.stem: Using E°: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V, I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V, which reaction is predicted to occur when iron(III) and iodide solutions are mixed?
options: No reaction, as both are oxidising agents
2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂
2Fe²⁺ + I₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻
Fe³⁺ + 3I⁻ → Fe + 3I₂
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺ (+0.77 V) is a stronger oxidising agent than I₂ (+0.54 V), so Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ to iodine and is reduced to Fe²⁺. Fe³⁺ is not reduced all the way to iron metal by iodide.

questions.stem: Use E°: Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V. Can copper(II) sulfate solution be stored safely in an iron container?
options: No, because Cu²⁺ ions reduce the iron to Fe²⁺ ions
Yes, because iron is less reactive than copper metal
No, because iron reduces Cu²⁺ ions, so the container corrodes
Yes, because Cu²⁺ ions are too weak to oxidise iron metal
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ is higher in the table than Fe²⁺, so Cu²⁺ oxidises iron: Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu. The container would dissolve while copper is deposited. Iron is oxidised, not reduced, in this reaction.

questions.stem: Standard electrode potentials predict that a metal should react with an acid, but no change is seen after an hour. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The reaction has reached equilibrium immediately, so no change is seen
E° values predict reactions in reverse when solutions are not 1 mol L⁻¹
The reaction is very slow, as E° values give no information about rate
The E° values only apply when the reaction is carried out in a galvanic cell
questions.explanation: E° values show whether a reaction tends to occur under standard conditions, not how fast it goes. A reaction can be favoured yet have a high activation energy, or be slowed by a protective oxide layer, as with aluminium.

questions.stem: Which energy conversion takes place in a galvanic cell?
options: Electrical energy is converted to heat energy
Chemical energy is converted to electrical energy
Electrical energy is converted to chemical energy
Heat energy is converted to electrical energy
questions.explanation: A galvanic cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to push electrons through an external circuit. An electrolytic cell does the reverse, using electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction.

questions.stem: In a galvanic cell, at which electrode does oxidation occur, and what is its polarity?
options: The cathode, which is positive
The anode, which is negative
The anode, which is positive
The cathode, which is negative
questions.explanation: Oxidation always occurs at the anode. In a galvanic cell the anode releases electrons into the external circuit, so it is the negative electrode. In an electrolytic cell the anode is positive, but it is still the site of oxidation.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is made from Zn²⁺/Zn (E° = −0.76 V) and Cu²⁺/Cu (E° = +0.34 V) half-cells under standard conditions. What is the cell potential?
questions.explanation: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = +0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V. A spontaneous galvanic cell has a positive cell potential. Adding the values directly gives 0.42 V.

questions.stem: In a standard zinc-copper galvanic cell, in which direction do electrons flow?
options: Through the wire from the copper electrode to the zinc electrode
Through the salt bridge from the zinc half-cell to the copper half-cell
Through the salt bridge from the copper half-cell to the zinc half-cell
Through the wire from the zinc electrode to the copper electrode
questions.explanation: Zinc is oxidised at the anode, releasing electrons that travel through the external circuit to the copper cathode, where Cu²⁺ is reduced. Electrons never travel through the salt bridge; ions carry the charge there.

questions.stem: A zinc-copper galvanic cell has a salt bridge soaked in potassium nitrate solution. In which direction do the nitrate ions migrate?
options: Towards the zinc half-cell, where Zn²⁺ ions are forming
Towards the copper half-cell, where Cu²⁺ ions are forming
Towards the copper half-cell, where Zn²⁺ ions are forming
Towards the zinc half-cell, where Cu²⁺ ions are removed
questions.explanation: At the anode, Zn²⁺ ions enter the solution, building up positive charge, so anions such as NO₃⁻ migrate towards the zinc half-cell to keep it neutral. Cations such as K⁺ move towards the copper half-cell, where Cu²⁺ is being removed.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell has a silver half-cell containing Ag⁺(aq). Why is potassium nitrate used in the salt bridge rather than potassium chloride?
options: Nitrate ions carry more charge than chloride ions, so the current is larger
Potassium chloride is not soluble enough in water to conduct electricity
Chloride ions would precipitate silver chloride and remove Ag⁺ from the cell
Chloride ions would be oxidised by silver metal and stop the current flowing
questions.explanation: Salt-bridge ions must not react with the half-cell solutions. Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) would remove silver ions and block the bridge. Both nitrate and chloride carry a single negative charge, and potassium chloride is very soluble.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is built from Zn²⁺/Zn (E° = −0.76 V) and Ag⁺/Ag (E° = +0.80 V) half-cells under standard conditions. What is the cell potential?
questions.explanation: E°cell = +0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Doubling the silver value because two Ag⁺ ions are reduced per zinc atom gives 2.36 V, but E° values are not multiplied by coefficients.

questions.stem: Which cell diagram represents a galvanic cell with an iron anode in Fe²⁺(aq) and a silver cathode in Ag⁺(aq)?
options: Fe(s) | Ag⁺(aq) || Fe²⁺(aq) | Ag(s)
Fe(s) | Fe²⁺(aq) || Ag⁺(aq) | Ag(s)
Ag(s) | Ag⁺(aq) || Fe²⁺(aq) | Fe(s)
Fe²⁺(aq) | Fe(s) || Ag(s) | Ag⁺(aq)
questions.explanation: The anode is written on the left and the cathode on the right, with the double line for the salt bridge. Each half-cell is written in the order of its reaction: Fe → Fe²⁺ on the left and Ag⁺ → Ag on the right.

questions.stem: A half-cell contains a solution of Fe³⁺ and Fe²⁺ ions. Why is a platinum or graphite electrode used in it?
options: Iron metal would be reduced by the solution, so it cannot be used as an electrode
Neither ion is a solid conductor, so an inert electrode is needed to carry electrons
Platinum catalyses the reaction, so the cell potential becomes much more positive
Graphite reacts with Fe³⁺ ions to form iron metal, which then conducts the current
questions.explanation: When both species of a couple are dissolved, the half-cell needs a conductor that does not take part in the reaction. Platinum and graphite are inert, so they transfer electrons without changing the cell reaction or its potential.

questions.stem: A standard zinc-copper galvanic cell is run for several hours. How do the masses of the electrodes change?
options: The zinc electrode loses mass and the copper electrode gains mass
The zinc electrode gains mass and the copper electrode loses mass
Both electrodes lose mass as they dissolve into their solutions
Neither electrode changes mass, because only electrons move
questions.explanation: At the zinc anode, Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻, so zinc dissolves. At the copper cathode, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so copper is deposited.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a secondary cell, such as the lead-acid accumulator, from a primary cell, such as the Leclanché cell?
options: Its redox reaction can be reversed by recharging with an external power supply
It produces electricity from a non-spontaneous reaction driven by a power supply
Its reactants are supplied continuously from outside, so it never runs flat
It uses a liquid electrolyte, whereas every primary cell uses a dry paste
questions.explanation: A secondary cell can be recharged: an external supply drives the cell reaction backwards, regenerating the reactants. Continuous supply of reactants describes a fuel cell, and both types discharge by a spontaneous reaction.

questions.stem: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, which reaction occurs at the anode?
options: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻
O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
questions.explanation: Oxidation occurs at the anode, where hydrogen gas loses electrons to form hydrogen ions. Oxygen is reduced to water at the cathode, so the only product of the cell is water.

questions.stem: An iron nail is placed in each of three test tubes: one with dry air, one with boiled water sealed under oil, and one with ordinary tap water open to the air. In which tube does the nail rust?
options: Only the tube with tap water open to the air
Only the tube with boiled water under oil
Only the tube with dry air
All three tubes, at the same rate
questions.explanation: Rusting needs both oxygen and water: iron is oxidised (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) while oxygen is reduced in the water (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻). Dry air lacks water, and boiled water under oil has had its dissolved oxygen removed.

questions.stem: Blocks of zinc are bolted to the steel hull of a ship. How do they protect the hull from corrosion?
options: Zinc forms a coating that seals all the steel off from water and oxygen
Zinc reacts with oxygen in seawater, so no oxygen can reach the hull
Zinc is a stronger reducing agent, so it is oxidised instead of the iron
Zinc is a weaker reducing agent, so it forces iron to act as the cathode
questions.explanation: The zinc acts as a sacrificial anode. Being more easily oxidised than iron, it gives up electrons to the hull, which becomes the cathode and is protected. The blocks are used up and must be replaced.

questions.stem: Use E°: Sn²⁺/Sn −0.14 V, Fe²⁺/Fe −0.44 V. A tin-plated steel can is scratched through to the steel. Why does the exposed iron then rust faster than unplated steel would?
options: Tin reacts with water to release hydrogen ions, which attack the exposed steel
Iron is the stronger reducing agent, so it becomes the anode and tin the cathode
Tin is the stronger reducing agent, so it becomes the anode and iron the cathode
Tin catalyses the reduction of iron, so iron ions are reduced to iron metal
questions.explanation: Iron has the more negative E°, so where the two metals touch in moist air, iron is oxidised and tin acts as the cathode where oxygen is reduced. Tin protects only while the coating is unbroken; zinc, which is more reactive than iron, protects even when scratched.

questions.stem: In impressed-current cathodic protection of a steel pipeline, how is the pipeline connected?
options: To the positive terminal of a DC supply, making it the anode
To a block of copper, which is oxidised instead of the iron
To the negative terminal of a DC supply, making it the anode
To the negative terminal of a DC supply, making it the cathode
questions.explanation: Connecting the steel to the negative terminal supplies it with electrons, so it acts as a cathode where reduction, not oxidation, occurs. An inert or scrap-metal anode is connected to the positive terminal. Copper is a weaker reducing agent than iron and would speed up corrosion.

questions.stem: What does an electrolytic cell do?
options: It uses a salt bridge to keep the oxidising and reducing agents apart
It uses heat from the surroundings to drive an endothermic redox reaction
It uses an external power supply to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction
It uses a spontaneous redox reaction to supply electricity to a circuit
questions.explanation: An electrolytic cell is supplied with electrical energy, which forces a reaction with a negative cell potential to occur. A spontaneous reaction producing electricity is a galvanic cell.

questions.stem: In an electrolytic cell, which electrode is negative, and what happens there?
options: The cathode, where oxidation occurs
The anode, where reduction occurs
The cathode, where reduction occurs
The anode, where oxidation occurs
questions.explanation: The cathode is connected to the negative terminal of the power supply, which pushes electrons onto it, so species are reduced there. The polarities are opposite to those of a galvanic cell, but oxidation is still at the anode.

questions.stem: Inert electrodes are used to electrolyse molten sodium chloride. Which products form, and where?
options: Sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Chlorine at the cathode and sodium at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explanation: Na⁺ ions move to the negative cathode and are reduced to sodium metal, while Cl⁻ ions move to the positive anode and are oxidised to chlorine gas. With no water present, no hydrogen or oxygen can form.

questions.stem: In the electrolytic refining of copper, impure copper containing zinc, iron, silver and gold is the anode. What happens to these impurities?
options: Silver and gold dissolve and stay in solution; zinc and iron plate onto the cathode
Zinc and iron dissolve as ions and stay in solution; silver and gold fall as anode sludge
Zinc and iron fall as anode sludge; silver and gold dissolve and plate onto the cathode
All four metals dissolve as ions and are deposited with the copper onto the cathode
questions.explanation: Zinc and iron are stronger reducing agents than copper, so they are oxidised at the anode, but their ions are harder to reduce than Cu²⁺ and stay in solution. Silver and gold are weaker reducing agents, so they are not oxidised and fall to the bottom as sludge. Only pure copper is deposited at the cathode.

questions.stem: A steel spoon is to be electroplated with silver. How should the cell be set up?
options: Spoon as the anode, silver as the cathode, and an electrolyte containing Ag⁺ ions
Spoon as the cathode, silver as the anode, and an electrolyte containing Fe²⁺ ions
Spoon as the anode, graphite as the cathode, and an electrolyte containing Na⁺ ions
Spoon as the cathode, silver as the anode, and an electrolyte containing Ag⁺ ions
questions.explanation: Silver must be deposited on the spoon, so the spoon is the cathode where Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. The silver anode dissolves (Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻), replacing the Ag⁺ removed from the electrolyte.
